He is making a **negating / "hold it" gesture — the everyday "no, no" wave**. Standing as
the official (umpire) beside the stump, he raises both hands with the palms turned outward
and sweeps his flat open right hand back and forth across in front of his face while
talking to the bowler. In context this reads as **"no — stop / wait, don't bowl yet"**
(equivalently "no, no — leave it / never mind"): he is waving the action off for a moment
rather than making any formal scoring signal. A beat later he drops his hands, claps to
signal that things are ready, and the bowler immediately runs in and bowls.

## The scene, so the gesture can be read in context

- The video is a night-time game of improvised street cricket played on a closed-off,
  freshly resurfaced London road (the "Cromwell Tower" sign of the Barbican Estate and a
  City of London crest are visible in the background, along with roadworks plant, pallets
  of paving, workers with brooms and orange plastic barriers).
- The "wicket" is a single light-blue plastic stump in a blue plastic base, with a white
  crease line painted on the tarmac; a proper set of stumps stands further down the road at
  the other end (visible when the camera pans right at the end of the clip).
- The man in question is young, in a blue shirt and a grey/khaki waistcoat, with an event ID
  card on a lanyard. He stands just behind and to the side of the stump at the bowler's
  end — the umpire's/official's position.
- The bowler is the man on the left in the black T-shirt, khaki chinos and white trainers,
  also wearing a lanyard, holding a yellow ball in both hands and waiting to start his
  run-up.

## Exactly what he does, frame by frame

- **0.0–0.3 s:** his right hand is up at chin level, palm down, and his arms move across his
  chest; he then swings the right arm out to his side.
- **0.3–0.55 s:** both hands come up to head/shoulder height with the palms facing outward —
  the classic "whoa, hold on" posture. The right hand is held flat and vertical in front of
  his face; his mouth is moving, i.e. he is speaking at the same time.
- **0.55–0.8 s:** the flat right hand sweeps horizontally right across in front of his face
  (it blurs straight over his nose and eyes in the frames at ~0.6–0.7 s) and carries on out
  to the other side.
- **0.8–0.95 s:** the arm finishes extended out sideways at chest/shoulder height, then he
  brings his hands back in.
- **~1.0–2.3 s:** he claps his hands repeatedly.
- **~1.9–2.5 s:** the bowler runs in and delivers the ball; the camera then pans right to
  follow the play.

Throughout the wave his head is turned to his right (screen left) and slightly down — he is
looking at the bowler and the group standing at that end, **not** at the camera.

## Why that adds up to "no / stop / wait"

- An open palm held up and waved from side to side in front of the face is the near-universal
  sign of negation or refusal: "no", "no thanks", "don't", "stop". Both palms raised outward
  at the same time reinforces the "hold on / calm down" reading.
- The addressee is clear: he is looking at and speaking to the bowler, who is standing ready
  with the ball in hand. Nothing had yet been bowled in the clip, so he is dealing with the
  moment *before* the delivery — holding it up.
- The sequel confirms it: as soon as he has finished the wave he claps encouragingly, and
  only then does the bowler start his run-up and bowl. The wave was "not yet / no"; the clap
  was "right, we're ready — come on".

## What it is not

- It is **not** a formal cricket umpire's signal. It matches none of them: four is a sweep of
  the arm across the chest after a ball has been hit (no ball had been bowled yet), a wide is
  both arms held straight out horizontally, out is a raised index finger, dead ball is the
  wrists crossed and uncrossed below the waist, and a cancelled call is the arms crossed onto
  the shoulders. His movement is ordinary conversational body language, not a scoring signal
  to a scorer.
- It is **not** him fanning himself or wafting away a smell or insects: both arms are raised
  and the hand travels in one large sweep across the face while he talks to someone, rather
  than fluttering back and forth close to his own face.
- It is **not** a greeting or a "don't film me" wave at the camera operator: he is turned
  away from the camera, facing and addressing the bowler to his right.

## Confidence

The gesture itself — an emphatic hand-waved negation/"hold on" aimed at the bowler and the
people at his end, followed by an "off you go" clap — is clear from the footage. The precise
words behind it cannot be recovered (the clip has no audio track at all), so whether he means
specifically "no, wait, not yet" or "no, no, forget it / don't worry about that" is an
inference from the surrounding action; both are the same underlying message of negation.
